studies.title: Held In The Source Book
studies.meaning: An oath is sworn by the Book that makes things clear, and what follows is a claim about where this recitation exists. It was made an Arabic recitation so people could use their minds on it, and it is also with God in what the ayah calls the source of the Book, described as high and wise. Commentators read that as an original the recited version corresponds to. Then a question with no answer supplied: shall We simply turn the Reminder away from you because you are a people who go too far.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, opening a surah whose name comes from a word about gold ornament much later in it. The audience had already refused the message repeatedly, which is what the final question is built on. Commentators note that the surah opens by insisting the message will not be withdrawn, which sets its tone: what follows is argument and satire rather than a threat of removal. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: Arabic uses the word for mother to mean the origin or main body of something. The same phrase occurs in two other surahs, once for the clear ayat and once for what God confirms and erases.
From a root meaning to tie or tether an animal. Understanding in this vocabulary is binding things together so they do not wander off, which is why it is offered as the purpose of a language.
A noun for turning the side or face away from someone. It occurs only here, and its root also supplies the word for overlooking a fault, so the gesture can mean dismissal or forgiveness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Important agreements in Mecca were often written and deposited, and a document kept in the sanctuary carried more weight than any recitation of its terms. The Quraysh had done exactly this with a boycott agreement against the Prophet's clan. An audience used to the difference between a stored original and a spoken copy would have heard the claim in this passage in familiar administrative terms.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the source of the Book occurs three times in the Quran, and each time in a different grammatical case in a different surah. In one it names the plain ayat that anchor the rest, in another it sits beside a statement about what God erases and confirms, and here it names where this recitation is kept.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places the revelation in two locations at once, one recited in a particular language and one held at the source. That distinction lets the text be genuinely Arabic without being merely local. It also makes the closing question the sharpest thing in the passage: withdrawal is presented as the reasonable response to a people who go too far, and it is not the response taken. The continued availability of the message is being named as unearned.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for the ayat that anchor the Book, distinguishing them from those open to more than one reading.
Places the same source of the Book with God, alongside what He erases and what He fixes in place.
Describes the recitation as glorious and kept in a guarded tablet, another statement about where it is held.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of the Quran today with the question this passage puts at its centre: what would it be like if this were withdrawn. Not permanently, just for a year. Notice how quickly the thought becomes uncomfortable, and notice that the surah opens by raising the possibility and declining it.

studies.title: Not One Escaped The Mockery
studies.meaning: Four lines that build a pattern and then puncture it. How many prophets were sent to earlier peoples, and not one arrived without being ridiculed; the exception is stated as an absolute. Commentators note that mockery, not argument, is named as the standard reception. Then the reminder that stronger peoples were destroyed, and their example has already passed by. The last line turns to the present audience with a question they cannot dodge: ask them who made the heavens and the earth, and they will name the Mighty, the Knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh acknowledged a supreme creator while directing their worship elsewhere, which is the contradiction the fourth line exposes. Commentators treat the survey of earlier prophets as consolation for the Prophet and warning for his audience at once. The ruins of earlier Arabian peoples lay along the trade roads north, so the reference to destroyed communities was geographically concrete rather than legendary.

keyTerms.note: A particle of quantity used for emphasis rather than counting. It opens a claim about scale without committing to a number, which is how the Quran usually introduces the earlier peoples.
A verb for making a joke of someone in company. It names a social technique rather than an intellectual position, which is why the Quran reports it as the standard reception.
A noun for seizing hard and striking. Comparing earlier peoples by this rather than by wealth or numbers measures them in the one currency the audience respected most.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The road north from Mecca to Syria passed abandoned settlements and rock-cut tombs left by peoples the Arabs named in their poetry. Caravans camped near them. The dead cities were part of the mental furniture of anyone who had travelled that route, and referring to communities stronger than the Quraysh who no longer existed was pointing at something the audience had ridden past.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here to compare earlier peoples by their violent strength occurs twice in the Quran, and both times in surahs of this period addressing the same objection. The Quran repeatedly makes its comparison in terms of force rather than wealth or numbers, matching the value its audience actually used when ranking one people against another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies ridicule as the characteristic response to prophecy, which reframes what a believer should expect. Being laughed at is not evidence of being wrong; it is the reported norm. The final line then isolates the real problem. These people already know who made the heavens and the earth, so the dispute is not about information. What separates them from the message is not a fact they lack.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule about messengers, that no messenger came to them without being mocked.
Records the same admission about who created the heavens and earth, and asks how they are turned away.
Tells the Prophet that messengers before him were ridiculed, and what surrounded those who mocked them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a conviction you hold that you have softened in company because you expected to be laughed at. Say it once this week without the softening, to one person who will not take it well. The ayah does not promise the mockery is wrong about you. It says the mockery is what happened to everybody who spoke.

studies.title: The Earth Made A Cradle
studies.meaning: Two provisions with the same structure: something given, and a purpose attached. The earth was made a cradle, and paths were traced across it, so that you might find your way. Water comes down in measure, and a dead region is revived by it, and the sentence ends with the conclusion drawn out of that: thus will you be brought forth. Commentators note the shift from second person to first person and back inside these two lines, which keeps the natural process and the divine act from separating.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's opening argument, which lists what the audience already acknowledges before showing what they refuse. Resurrection was the specific point of Meccan resistance, and the Quran answers it here from rainfall rather than by assertion. Commentators report no occasion. The word for a dead region rather than a dead field fits a landscape where whole districts, not just fields, went green or stayed bare.

keyTerms.note: The word for an infant's cot and for ground smoothed and prepared. It occurs twice in the Quran, and its choice makes the earth a place arranged for something helpless rather than simply inhabited.
The plural of the ordinary word for a road. Naming the passes and valley routes as something placed rather than found makes the possibility of travel a provision rather than a feature of terrain.
An exact quantity rather than a limit. Rain that is measured is rain fitted to what a place can take, which distinguishes it from both drought and the flood the Quran describes elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Routes through the Hijaz were not obvious. Between ranges of black rock, the passable ways were specific and known, and a guide's value lay in holding them in memory. Losing the path meant losing the wells that went with it. Describing the roads as laid down rather than discovered would have struck people who paid guides handsomely for knowledge that felt like a kind of gift.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the earth as a cradle occurs twice in the Quran, once here and once in an account of Moses; a closely related form appears once more in a short surah asking whether the earth was not made a bed. The image of the ground as bedding for the human being is built from three words that never repeat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage builds its case for resurrection out of things nobody disputes, which is its method throughout. A cradle, a road and a rainfall are not contested. What is contested is the conclusion, and the ayah simply attaches it to the same sentence as the rainfall rather than arguing for it separately. That placement is the argument: the same act that revives a district is being described as the pattern for what comes later.

crossReferences.why: Lists the earth as a bed and sleep as rest in the same catalogue, using a closely related word for the ground.
Uses the same word for the earth as a cradle, in Moses answering a question about who his Lord is.
Ends the same comparison with the phrase that such is the coming forth, joining rain to resurrection.

studies.applyIt: Look up the name of one road you use every week and find out when it was built and by whom. Then notice how much of your life runs along routes you did not choose or make. This passage calls paths a provision, and the claim is easier to test on a road with a date than on an idea.

studies.title: Words For The Moment You Settle
studies.meaning: Pairs were created, all of them, and ships and livestock were provided to ride. Then the passage does something unusual: it specifies a moment and supplies the words for it. When you have settled onto their backs, remember your Lord's favour and say that glory belongs to the one who put this at our service, since we could never have brought it under control ourselves. Commentators note the exactness of the timing, after mounting rather than before, when the animal is under you and the effort of getting there is finished.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Camels and ships were the two things that made long-distance trade possible, and the audience's wealth rested on both. The words given here entered later Muslim practice as a supplication said when setting out, which the classical sources record. Commentators report no specific occasion for the ayat. Their placement in the surah's list of acknowledged favours sets up the accusation that follows about ingratitude.

keyTerms.note: A plural covering matched pairs and, by extension, sorts and species. Saying all of them makes the claim total, so nothing that comes in pairs falls outside what is described.
A verb for coming to rest level and balanced. It marks the exact moment after mounting when a rider stops adjusting, which is when the passage tells him to speak.
From the root for a rope tying two things together, so the sense is being strong enough to hold something down beside you. It occurs only here in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mounting a loaded camel was a small operation. The animal had to be couched, the load balanced, the rider settled before it rose, and a badly mounted beast could throw a man or spill a season's goods. Everyone had watched it go wrong. The moment the passage names, when you are finally seated and steady, was a real and recognisable pause in a working day.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing what a rider could never do to a mount by his own strength occurs only in this ayah. The phrase given here to be said on mounting became a widely used travelling supplication, and the classical collections record it being said by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) when he set his foot in the stirrup, with the following ayah added to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches remembrance to a physical position rather than to a mood, which makes it repeatable. Gratitude here is not something summoned but something triggered by the body arriving somewhere. It also names the specific illusion that the moment invites: a man seated on a large animal that is obeying him feels competent, and the words supplied cut directly across that feeling without denying the competence.

crossReferences.why: Names the loaded ship as a sign and says similar vessels were created for them to ride.
Lists the livestock with their warmth, uses and beauty, and the animals given for carrying loads.
Gives Noah words to say once settled on the ark, a supplication tied to the same act of boarding.

studies.applyIt: Choose one moment of settling that happens every day: sitting down in the car, taking your seat on the train, closing the front door behind you. Say one sentence of thanks at that exact point, the same sentence each time. This passage does not ask for a feeling. It picks a posture and attaches words to it.

studies.title: A Portion Of His Own Servants
studies.meaning: The traveller's words finish with a return to the Lord, and then the surah turns sharply. They assign Him a portion out of His own servants, which commentators explain as making created beings into a share of God Himself. Human ingratitude is named as plainly as anywhere in the Quran. The third line puts the matter as a question with an edge: has He taken daughters from what He creates and singled you out for sons. The absurdity is left to do its own work, without a counter-argument attached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some Arabs regarded the angels as God's daughters and made them objects of appeal, while placing a high value on sons in their own households. Commentators identify this double standard as the target of these lines. The Quran returns to it in several surahs of this period. No specific occasion is reported, and the argument is presented as an exposure rather than a rebuttal.

keyTerms.note: A verb for being turned over or flipped, used of returning by the way you came. It makes the return a reversal of direction rather than an arrival somewhere new.
The word for a part cut from a whole. Using it for what people attributed to God frames the error as division rather than as adding something alongside Him.
From a root for purity and for choosing the clearest part of something. The verb carries preference, which is what makes the question sting: they claim the better share for themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance in Arabia divided an estate into portions, and every family knew the arithmetic of who took what. A share was a concrete thing, argued over and counted out. Using the vocabulary of a portion for what people attributed to God put the claim into the language of an estate division, where taking a piece necessarily reduces the whole.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a portion in this ayah belongs to the vocabulary of dividing something up, and the same root gives the term later used for the thirty sections a copy of the Quran is divided into for reading. A word for cutting a whole into parts sits in this ayah as the description of a theological error.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage handles a doctrinal claim by exposing what it implies rather than by refuting it. If God has a portion drawn from His creation, then He is the kind of thing that has parts, and the whole argument follows from that. The second half then shifts to the arguer rather than the argument. A belief that quietly assigns the less valued option to God tells you more about the believer than about God.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question about daughters directly, and says they are lying when they claim God has begotten.
Asks whether the male is yours and the female His, calling that an unfair division of shares.
Answers the whole line of thinking by denying begetting and being begotten in the shortest possible form.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you give away readily and one you keep back, in any part of your life: which invitations you accept, which tasks you volunteer for, which possessions you lend. Line them up honestly. This passage judges people by what they were willing to assign elsewhere, and the pattern is usually visible before you go looking for it.

studies.title: His Face Goes Dark
studies.meaning: The argument becomes a scene. One of them is told the news of what he has just attributed to the Merciful, meaning a daughter, and his face darkens while he swallows his grief. Then a quoted objection in his own voice: one brought up among ornaments, and not clear in a dispute. Commentators read the two clauses as the two grounds of contempt, decoration and no use in an argument. The passage does not answer the objection. It records the man's reaction and leaves the contradiction standing in his own words.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran describes elsewhere the shame of a father hearing that a daughter had been born, and it names and condemns the burying of infant girls. Commentators tie this passage to that setting. The wider argument is about angels being called God's daughters by people who would not want daughters themselves, and this scene supplies the evidence rather than the doctrine.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a colour deepening, describing a face going dark with anger or grief. It is a physical description offered instead of a report of his feelings, which the ayah adds separately.
From a root for tying a waterskin's mouth shut so nothing escapes. The word is used of Jacob's grief for Joseph, and it names holding something in rather than not feeling it.
The word for worked jewellery, occurring only here in this form. The complaint is that she is raised among such things, which the objector treats as evidence of what she is for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A daughter in a raiding society was a dependent who could not fight and whose marriage meant a negotiation with another clan. Sons defended a household and inherited its standing. The contempt in this quoted line was not a private prejudice but an economic reading of a person, and it was said openly. What the Quran does is repeat it back in the speaker's own words.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for choked-back grief in this ayah occurs three times in the Quran. One is Jacob turning away from his sons with his eyes white from sorrow over Joseph, and another describes the same darkened face at news of a daughter in a different surah. The Quran uses one word for a father's grief that is honoured and a father's shame that is condemned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage exposes a contradiction by dramatising it rather than naming it. A man attributes daughters to God and cannot bear one himself; nothing more needs to be said. It also quietly takes the daughter's side without ever addressing her, since the description of the father is unflattering in every clause. And the objection quoted, that she is decorative and no use in argument, is left to sound as thin as it is.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same darkened face and adds the man hiding from his people over the news he received.
Names the buried infant girl and asks for what offence she was killed, in the reckoning scenes.
Uses the same word for suppressed grief, of Jacob turning away with his eyes whitened over Joseph.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose worth you assess by what they can do for you rather than by who they are: a colleague, a relative you find tiring, someone who serves you regularly. Say their name and one thing about them that is true and useless to you. This passage is about a man who could only see a function.

studies.title: Were They There To Watch
studies.meaning: The claim is stated with a correction built into it: they made the angels, who are servants of the Merciful, females. Naming them servants first settles their standing before the objection is raised. Then a question about method rather than content. Did they witness their creation. Commentators point out that the challenge is evidential, not theological: whatever anyone says about beings they have never seen made is testimony given without observation. The line closes by saying the testimony is being recorded, and that they will be asked about it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Several Arabian tribes treated angels as female intermediaries who could carry a request to God, and shrines were maintained on that basis. Commentators identify this passage as addressing that belief. The Quran's response across this surah is consistent: it asks where the information came from rather than debating the metaphysics. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A phrase placed inside the sentence before the objection, so the angels' status is fixed as service. The Quran uses the same phrase later for a category of human beings as well.

keyTerms.gloss: were they present, did they witness
keyTerms.note: A verb combining being present and giving testimony. Asking it of a creation nobody attended turns a religious claim into an evidential one, which is the argument's whole move.
The future passive of the ordinary verb for writing. Casual speech is treated as a deposition being entered into a record, which is what makes the closing clause weigh so much.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony in Arabia was oral and personal. A witness had to have been present, and a man who spoke about what he had not seen could be discredited by the simple question of where he had been standing. Written records existed for debts and treaties and carried a different, heavier authority. The ayah moves a spoken claim into the written category, which its audience would have felt as a change of stakes.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the angels, servants of the Merciful, reappears much later in the Quran as the title of a long passage describing believing human beings by their conduct. The same two words name the angels in this ayah and a kind of person in another surah, which places both inside one category of service rather than in separate ranks.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a standard of evidence for religious claims and applies it without exception. Anything asserted about the unseen has to come from somewhere, and the ayah asks the question directly. It also treats speech as consequential rather than idle. What people say about God is being entered into a record they will be questioned on, which raises the cost of repeating something merely because it is commonly said.

crossReferences.why: Opens the long passage that gives the same phrase to human beings, describing how the servants of the Merciful walk.
Asks whether they were present when the angels were created, putting the same evidential challenge directly.
Forbids pursuing what you have no knowledge of, and says hearing, sight and heart will be questioned.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have repeated about religion because you heard it somewhere. Try to name where. If you cannot, either find out this week or stop saying it. This ayah is not against believing things on report; it is against not knowing which of your beliefs are on report and which you have actually checked.

studies.title: They Are Only Guessing
studies.meaning: The argument quoted is a real one and it is not answered on its own terms. Had the Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them. Commentators note that the statement is true as a proposition and useless as a defence, since it explains nothing about the speaker's own choices. What the ayah says is that they have no knowledge of this; they are only estimating. The word used is for guessing at a quantity you cannot count, so the charge is not that they are lying but that they are treating a guess as a foundation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a run of quoted objections that the surah answers one after another. This one appears in similar words in other Meccan surahs, which suggests it was a settled argument rather than a stray remark. Commentators note that the Quran neither accepts nor denies the underlying claim about divine will here; it addresses the speakers' basis for advancing it. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A conditional that the Quran uses often in its own voice about matters that were arranged otherwise. Here it is quoted from opponents, where the same construction becomes an excuse rather than an explanation.
Given indefinitely and negated, so the sentence says they have not even a scrap of it. The Quran regularly measures a claim by this standard before addressing whether it is true.
A verb for reckoning the yield of a palm tree by eye before the harvest. It names approximation done for practical reasons, which is a poor foundation for a claim about God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Estimating a date harvest by eye was a real practice with a real name. A man walked through a grove before picking and judged what it would yield, and the figure was used for dividing shares. Everyone accepted the method and everyone knew it was approximate. Naming a religious argument with that word placed it in a category people already understood as good enough for dates and nothing more.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for guessing occurs three times in the Quran in this exact form, and each closes a sentence about people following assumption where knowledge was needed; two of the three concern invoking something besides God. Its everyday sense is estimating the fruit still on a palm tree before it is picked.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to settle the question of divine will and human action, and that refusal is deliberate. What it addresses is a use of the question rather than the question itself. An argument invoked only to explain away one's own conduct is being treated as a symptom rather than a position. That leaves the underlying difficulty genuinely open, which is where the classical tradition largely leaves it too.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same argument at greater length and answers it with the same charge of following mere conjecture.
Records the identical excuse and replies that the messengers' duty was only clear delivery.
Says conjecture avails nothing against the truth, stating the principle this ayah applies to a particular case.

studies.applyIt: Take one belief you hold about why your life has gone the way it has. Ask whether you would be able to say where the knowledge came from if someone pressed. This ayah does not tell the speakers they are wrong. It tells them they do not know, which is a different and more uncomfortable finding.

studies.title: We Found Our Fathers On A Way
studies.meaning: A question first: have We given them a book before this one that they are holding on to. The answer is not supplied because the next line supplies it for them. No, they say: we found our fathers on a way, and we are guided by their tracks. Commentators note the exact claim being made. They are not saying inheritance is enough; they are calling the inheritance guidance. The word for what the fathers were on is unusual, naming a community and a course at once, so a people and a path are treated as the same thing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Quraysh authority rested on custom rather than on any text, which is what makes the first question sharp: no earlier scripture supported their practice and everyone knew it. Commentators read this exchange as the surah's central diagnosis of the opposition. The same claim is quoted in several places across the Quran, always in nearly the same words, which suggests it was the standard reply.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form for gripping something and not letting go. The image is a hand closed around a text, which is exactly what the questioners cannot produce when asked.
The word normally means a people or a generation, and here it carries the sense of a course they were on. The overlap is the point: the group and the path are not distinguished.
The active participle of being guided. Claiming it for oneself on the basis of following tracks is what the passage isolates, since the word normally implies arriving where you meant to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a genuine skill in the desert and a respected one. A man could read from prints how many had passed, how heavily loaded, and how long ago, and following tracks to water was a survival technique rather than a metaphor. The claim to be guided by ancestral footprints borrowed the prestige of that skill, which is what makes the answer in the next ayat necessary.
studies.didYouKnow: This claim about finding the fathers on a way is quoted twice in consecutive ayat of this surah with one word changed at the end. Here the speakers say they are rightly guided by the tracks; in the next ayah earlier peoples say only that they are following them. The stronger word belongs to the present audience, not to the ancients.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates inheritance from guidance without dismissing inheritance. The question about an earlier book leaves room for a tradition that does rest on revelation; what is refused is the move that turns descent itself into evidence. It also identifies where the difficulty actually sits. These people were not indifferent to guidance; they were confident they already had it, which is a harder position to reach from than not caring at all.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same reply and asks what if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided.
Records the same appeal to what the fathers followed, even if the devil were calling them to the Fire.
Gives the same answer to a call toward revelation, saying what they found their fathers on is enough.

studies.applyIt: Name one practice you keep because your family kept it, and one you keep because you looked into it. Be honest about which list is longer. You are not being asked to drop anything from the first list. You are being asked to know which list a thing is on before you defend it to somebody.

studies.title: The Comfortable Always Answered First
studies.meaning: A pattern is stated with an exception clause and no exceptions. No warner was ever sent to any town without those living in ease saying the same sentence: we found our fathers on a way and we are following in their footsteps. Commentators note the word identifying the speakers. It names people softened by comfort, and it specifies who did the objecting: not the poor of the town, not everyone in it, but those with the most to lose. The argument about ancestors turns out to have a consistent social address.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The leading families of Mecca controlled the sanctuary and the trade that came with it, and the earliest response to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) came disproportionately from those with little standing. Commentators connect this ayah to that division. The claim being made is historical and general: the same class objected in every town, which places the Quraysh leadership in a long line rather than in a special position.

keyTerms.note: From a root for being softened by abundance. The word describes comfort that has done something to a person, not simply wealth held, which is why the Quran uses it of a disposition.
One who gives notice of what is coming. The Quran uses it for prophets when their function is the message's urgency rather than its content, which suits a line about how they were received.
A verb for taking someone as a model to copy. It occurs only here, and it claims less than the word the present audience used one ayah earlier, which claimed guidance outright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The families that ran Mecca held offices attached to the sanctuary: providing water for pilgrims, holding the keys, feeding visitors, keeping the banner. These were hereditary, lucrative and inseparable from the religious arrangements a warner would disturb. Their objection to a new message was not only intellectual, and everyone in the city could see the accounts involved.
studies.didYouKnow: The word naming the objectors as those softened by ease occurs twice in the Quran in this exact form, and both times it identifies who rejected a messenger. A related form appears elsewhere for those a town's destruction begins with. The Quran consistently attaches this particular word to the same social position and the same response.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a sociological observation and lets it carry theological weight. Resistance to a message that would rearrange things concentrates among those the current arrangement favours, and the Quran states this as a rule rather than an accusation. That has an uncomfortable edge for any reader who is comfortable. It does not say the argument from ancestors is wrong because the wealthy make it, but it does note who makes it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other occurrence of the same word, with those living in ease claiming their wealth proves them favoured.
Uses a related form, describing the ease-softened of a town as where a community's undoing begins.
Shows the objection from the other side, a people asking Noah whether they should believe when the lowest have.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you would actually lose if something you believe were shown to be mistaken: money, standing, a role, a friendship. Write the list without deciding anything about the belief. This ayah names who objects rather than what they say, and knowing your own stake is the only defence against it applying to you.

studies.title: Even If I Bring You Better
studies.meaning: The warner's reply is a single question and it grants everything before challenging it. Even if I bring you better guidance than what you found your fathers on. He does not dispute that they found their fathers on something, and he does not call it worthless; he offers a comparison. Their answer refuses the comparison rather than losing it: we reject what you have been sent with. Commentators note the shift from a claim about ancestors to a flat statement about the messenger. The argument is dropped the moment it might be tested.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's exchange about inherited practice before it turns to Abraham, who broke with his own father's religion. Commentators read the placement as deliberate: the reply to inherited custom is not an argument but an example. The reply quoted here is given in the past tense about earlier warners, which makes the Quraysh answer to the Prophet a repetition of something already recorded.

keyTerms.note: A compound particle that concedes and challenges at once. It grants the previous statement and then asks whether it would still hold under a condition, which is the whole shape of the reply.
A comparative form of the word for guided. Offering a comparison rather than a contradiction leaves the fathers' way with some value, which is a more generous move than the answer it receives.
From the root for covering something over. The reply is not that the offer fails but that it will not be examined, which is what the root's sense of covering describes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a town of comparison. Merchants weighed one route against another, poets were ranked at the seasonal fairs, and buyers compared goods openly before committing. The habit of assessing which of two things was better was thoroughly familiar. What the warner asks for is the ordinary commercial courtesy of a comparison, and what he receives is a refusal to look.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative used here for better guidance appears across the Quran mostly in questions and challenges rather than in statements. In this ayah it is offered by a warner and never taken up, and the reply that follows changes the subject entirely, from what the fathers were on to what the messenger was sent with. The exchange records an argument being abandoned rather than lost.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies refusal as a decision separate from disagreement. The objectors do not claim the offered guidance is worse; they decline to weigh it. That distinction matters because it locates the difficulty in the will rather than in the evidence, which is where this surah keeps placing it. It also shows a messenger conceding as much as he honestly can, and getting nothing back for the concession.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same challenge to the same claim, asking what if their fathers understood nothing at all.
Follows immediately with Abraham declaring himself free of what his father and his people worshipped.
Shows the same refusal from another people, telling their prophet to bring on what he threatens.

studies.applyIt: Think of a view you hold that you have never actually compared with the best version of the alternative. Not a caricature of it, the strongest form you can find. Spend twenty minutes with that version this week. You may well keep your view. This ayah is about people who would not spend the twenty minutes.

studies.title: Is It They Who Apportion
studies.meaning: The question answers an objection quoted two ayat earlier, that a message of this weight should have come to a great man of one of the two cities. The reply shifts the ground: people who do not allocate even a livelihood are not the ones to allocate prophecy. The arrangement of rank is then given a purpose clause the commentators read as mutual employment, people taking one another into service, so difference of position is interlocking rather than a ladder of worth. The last clause sets a different currency against all of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The two cities were Mecca and Ta'if, and the objection was about standing: this should have arrived through a man with wealth and a following. The surah's name comes from ornaments of gold, and the ayat immediately after this imagine God furnishing the houses of those who reject the message with silver roofs and stairways, precisely in order to show how little such things settle.

keyTerms.note: The verb for dividing an inheritance or the meat of a slaughtered animal among claimants. It belongs to a world of visible shares, which is what makes the question about prophecy so pointed.
The plural of a step in a staircase. It names position on a scale without implying anything about worth, which is why the clause that follows has to state what the difference is for.
Read by the commentators as one another's labour being available for hire and exchange, not as ridicule. The reciprocal phrasing puts every rank on both sides of the arrangement at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's economy was a web of dependency: financiers, caravan leaders, guides who knew the wells, camel drivers, guards, water carriers, and the men who fed pilgrims through the season. Nobody in it worked alone, and the wealthiest households were the ones most dependent on other people's labour. The phrase about taking one another into service described the visible structure of the town.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is named after a word in the passage just after this one, where roofs of silver and stairways are imagined for the houses of those who reject the message, with the reason for withholding them given as the risk that everyone would then go the same way. Ornament is treated as so weak a mark of favour that it is nearly handed to the wrong side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are separated here that people habitually join: the distribution of livelihood, which is affirmed as God's doing, and the meaning of that distribution, which is denied any value as evidence about a person's standing. The reason given for difference of rank is functional rather than moral. And the closing clause names mercy as better than what is amassed, setting one against the other rather than ranking two goods.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same test running, the comfortable asking whether God really favoured these poor believers.
Takes the same fact about unequal provision and asks what those given more do with it.
Follows immediately, imagining silver roofs for those who reject and calling all of it the stuff of this life.

studies.applyIt: Name one person whose work you rely on and could not do yourself: whoever fixes the thing you use daily, whoever keeps a system running that you only notice when it stops. Thank them specifically this week, for the actual task. This ayah describes the arrangement as mutual, and mutual arrangements are usually only visible from one side.

studies.title: Friends Will Be Enemies
studies.meaning: The opening line is a statement about friendship rather than about enemies. On that day close friends turn on one another, and one group is excepted. The commentators read it as a claim about what the friendships were built on: those that held people to something survive, and those that helped people avoid it become accusations. Then the address shifts into the second person, fear and grief are both lifted, and the entry described is not solitary. Spouses go in together, which is stated as part of the welcome.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been describing a society defending inherited practice on the ground that the fathers did it, and describing companions who confirm one another in exactly that. This passage arrives after a statement in the voice of Jesus about worship and a straight path, and after a note that the parties differed among themselves. Friendship as a mechanism of drift is one of this surah's running concerns.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to penetrate or run all the way through something. Such a friend has entered a person's character rather than standing beside it, which is why the reversal described is so total.
The same word the Quran uses for matched pairs generally. Placing it inside the invitation makes the entry a shared arrival rather than an individual verdict delivered separately.
From a root joining beauty to gladness, related to the word for fine ornamented cloth. It describes joy that shows outwardly, the delight of someone being received well.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Friendship in Arabia was formal and public. Men were paired as companions for journeys and campaigns, and a person's reputation was shaped more by whose company they kept than by their own conduct, since observers had no other information to go on. Choosing companions was understood as choosing a direction, and families intervened in the choice. The word used here names the closest form of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for these friends comes from a root meaning to penetrate or permeate, because such a friend has got inside a person rather than remaining beside them. The same root gives the title the Quran uses of Abraham, who is called the intimate friend of God, so one word covers the highest and the most dangerous version of the same closeness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Friendship is treated as a moral instrument rather than as a private pleasure. The passage does not say that friendships end; it says they invert, which implies they were doing something all along that will eventually become visible. And the reversal is stated with an exception, so the remedy offered is not solitude. What changes the outcome is the character of the friendship rather than its existence.

crossReferences.why: Gives the regret from inside: a man who took someone as a friend and was turned from the reminder.
Uses the same word for Abraham, showing the closeness this ayah warns about at its best.
Describes the companion assigned to one who turns away, and the wish for distance on that day.

studies.applyIt: Think about which of your friendships produces the version of you that you would want recorded, and which produces the one you would not. You already know both answers. Put an hour in the calendar this month for the first person, by name, at a time. That is the whole exercise, and it is harder than it sounds.
